en: Mayon Volcano emits sulfur dioxide gas during eruptions, which reacts with rain to form acidic solutions.
The Chocolate Hills in Bohol are made of limestone, a solid sedimentary rock composed mainly of calcium carbonate.
The Philippine one-peso coin is made of nickel-plated steel, a material chosen because it resists the chemical change of rusting.
Abaca fibers from the Musa textilis plant undergo physical changes when cut and woven into strong Manila ropes.
The underground waters of the Puerto Princesa Subterranean River contain dissolved minerals, making it a homogeneous liquid solution.
San Agustin Church in Manila uses adobe stone, a solid material with great structural strength to support its heavy walls.
Tamarind pods contain tartaric acid, which dissolves in water to create the sour liquid solution used in sinigang.
The iron wheels of Philippine National Railways trains undergo a chemical change called oxidation when exposed to moist air.
The giant clam found in the Tubbataha Reef secretes calcium carbonate to build its hard, solid protective shell.
Burnay clay jars from Vigan undergo a chemical change when fired in a kiln, transforming soft clay into hard ceramic.
The white sand of Boracay Island consists of solid quartz grains that form a heterogeneous mixture when mixed with seawater.
The main crater lake of Taal Volcano contains liquid water that evaporates into a gaseous state under the hot sun.
